note: Sorted automatically from organic swipes (swipe-organic formats.py). Most rows are unreviewed.

rows.name: Sticky-line maker demo
rows.what: One text line pinned for the ENTIRE runtime while one continuous handheld demonstration plays out. The line never changes, so nothing competes with the product; the viewer re-reads it while watching hands work. Face is cropped or incidental — the maker is a pair of hands, not a personality.
rows.why_it_works: No cut to a talking head means no permission needed to keep watching. The unchanging line acts as the promise; every second of footage is evidence against it.

unfold / assemble — the scale reveal
place it where it lives (bed, counter, floor)
use it as intended, one unbroken take
close on the mechanism (switch, controller, texture) — the proof detail
extra.text_behaviour: one line, top third, same words start to finish, casual + an emoji or two; some instances land the line once on the opening beat and drop it, which does not break the format — what matters is that the text never changes and never argues
extra.camera: handheld phone, vertical, subject-height, natural window light, no cuts to face

rows.name: Objection-flip collection
rows.what: A quoted objection or question sits on screen the whole time with a two-word answer under it. One beat of human reaction, then the rest of the runtime is the PRODUCT COLLECTION as the answer — many units, ordered, filling a shelf or surface. The answer is objects, never words.
rows.why_it_works: It borrows the energy of an argument and settles it with abundance. The collection reads as proof of a life, not a purchase.

travel across the collection so the count registers

open it — the inside is the payoff
extra.text_behaviour: two lines pinned all runtime: the quoted objection in quotes, then 'Us:' + emoji answer
extra.camera: handheld, close orbit of the collection, natural interior light

rows.name: Forbidden tease → dark reveal
rows.what: Two acts with an environment switch at the seam. Act one: bright room, product hidden then unveiled, text warns you not to look ('Don't show this to a ___'). Act two: hard cut to darkness, where the product's whole value becomes visible, and the text switches from tease to a share command.
rows.why_it_works: The withheld thing is the mechanism, not the product. The dark cut is a physical reveal — the benefit literally cannot be seen until the room changes, so the viewer has to stay for it.

extra.text_behaviour: act one: 'Don't show this to a {identity}' + soft emoji · act two: 'Share this with a {identity}' — the switch lands on the cut
extra.camera: act one handheld daylight; act two locked or slow drift, exposure for the glow, everything else black

rows.name: Word-per-beat procedure
rows.what: A camera that never moves, held on the thing being treated. ONE WORD per beat builds a sentence across the whole video, one step of the procedure per word. The operator is hands only — or a swapped-in element standing in for them; the problem is the subject and stays in frame the entire time.
rows.why_it_works: The sentence is unfinished until the last beat, so the read is the retention device — you cannot leave mid-sentence. The unmoving frame on the problem means the before-state never leaves the screen while the fix happens.

extra.camera: zero camera movement — usually locked overhead on a reclined or seated subject, sometimes a locked frontal frame with the problem held at the edge of shot; even indoor light

rows.name: Filth-extraction montage
rows.what: The transformation is the DEBRIS, not the surface. One tool pulled across a filthy thing extracts a visible mat of gunk; then the same tool proves itself on three or four unrelated surfaces in quick succession; then it rinses clean. Often opens with a witness in frame reacting to how bad it is.
rows.why_it_works: Extracted filth is unfakeable evidence and physically satisfying. The multi-surface run turns one product into a household verdict instead of a single use case.

extra.camera: handheld, close on the contact point, daylight or plain interior light, cuts on each surface change

rows.name: Locked-frame escalating caption
rows.what: The camera never moves — one wide interior frame, product centred. Small quoted captions escalate beat by beat ('hate these' → 'you mean THIS one?' → 'THIS?' → 'this...?') while the product physically transforms further and further in the identical frame.
rows.why_it_works: Stillness makes change legible: because nothing else moves, every transformation reads instantly. The changing caption plays as a deadpan argument the product keeps winning.

extra.camera: tripod-locked wide, identical framing every beat, daylight through a window, never moves

rows.name: Character sketch
rows.what: One heightened costumed character carries the whole runtime. Wardrobe, hair and props do the satire before a word lands; dialogue finishes it. Zero on-screen text — the post caption carries the quoted punchline. A cast may react in cutaways and the character may stay in one confined location or roam between several; neither is load-bearing.
rows.why_it_works: People watch people, and a costume declares the whole premise in the first frame with no setup. Because it plays as a bit, the brand can be in the joke rather than interrupting it.

rows.name: Running caption over borrowed cutaways
rows.what: One continuous narration is chopped into per-beat caption fragments that never complete a sentence, and that running caption is the only thing holding together footage the creator did not shoot — someone else's clip, a published diagram, a screen recording, stock process footage. A small talking-head panel or cut-out is pinned somewhere in frame so the narrator never fully leaves.
rows.why_it_works: The caption is always mid-sentence, so there is never a clean place to leave. The borrowed material supplies authority and production value the creator could never shoot, and the persistent narrator panel makes it read as one argument instead of a scrapbook.

extra.camera: no camera of its own for most of the runtime — full-frame borrowed sources cut against a fixed studio or desk plate; the presenter panel never moves

rows.name: Split-screen mechanism verdict
rows.what: The frame is permanently divided for most of the runtime — the evidence in one band, the presenter in the other — so the viewer sees the claim and the person making it at the same second. The captions run the argument in order: correction, name, mechanism, verdict. The composite drops away only at the end, for the call.
rows.why_it_works: A split frame is an argument you cannot look away from: the ugly evidence never leaves the screen while the presenter reclassifies it. Because both halves are the same second, the mechanism is proved rather than asserted.

rows.name: Day-count self-test

rows.why_it_works: A date ledger converts a demo into a trial the viewer is auditing. Because the frame is identical every time, the only variable left is the thing being sold, so the change reads as caused rather than claimed.

rows.name: Reaction-panel repost
rows.what: Nothing in the post was shot for the post. Someone else's clip carries the whole runtime while a locked reaction panel of the poster sits in the frame the entire time and is never cut to. The reactor's presence, not their performance, is what licenses the borrowed clip.
rows.why_it_works: A real person visibly losing it is the fastest possible proof that the clip below is worth watching. The panel costs nothing to shoot and turns a repost into a post.

rows.name: Pinned line acted out
rows.what: One caption sets a premise and then the footage does nothing but perform it — literally, and further each beat. The line is pinned unchanged for the whole runtime (or lands once at the head and never returns); it is never completed in words. No product, no dialogue, no talking head — the body is the entire payload.
rows.why_it_works: The text makes a promise the footage can only settle physically, so every beat is the viewer checking the claim against the picture. Escalation gives the edit its own clock: each beat has to go further than the last or the joke dies.

extra.camera: no fixed rule and that is the point — a locked wide interior, a floor-level angle, or a freely roaming handheld covering a chain of gags; whatever holds the performance

rows.name: Deadpan reaction hold
rows.what: One frame is locked and simply held while a subject refuses to react. Everything else — a crowd, a second person, a label, the screen light — escalates around them, and the camera never cuts away or moves. The last third of the runtime is very often one unbroken close-up of a face doing nothing.
rows.why_it_works: A held non-reaction makes the viewer supply the missing emotion themselves, which is stickier than being handed it. Because the frame never moves, the length of the hold becomes the joke.

rows.name: Wordless single-take procedure
rows.what: One service delivered on one subject, in step order, with ZERO on-screen text anywhere and no cutaway, location change or graphic. The camera is close and handheld at the work's own level and reframes with the hands rather than sitting on a tripod. The payoff is physical — extracted debris, a peeled sheet held up to the lens, or the subject's involuntary reaction.
rows.why_it_works: Silence is the credential: nothing is being sold to you in words, so the only thing left to judge is what is visibly coming off. Holding on one subject for the whole runtime means the before-state is always still on screen when the payoff lands.

rows.name: Unfinished line, real payoff
rows.what: A caption defers its own answer — it trails off in an ellipsis, ends on an open colon, or is cut off mid-word — and is then pinned unchanged while wordless footage delivers the answer instead. The footage is one continuous unstaged take; the payoff is something real that happened, not something performed.
rows.why_it_works: An unfinished sentence is an open loop the viewer cannot close by reading, only by watching. Because the payoff is unstaged, it cannot be argued with, and the gap between the flat line and the real event is the whole joke.

rows.name: Labelled cutaway mechanism
rows.what: No person, no room, no product in hand — the whole runtime is one unmoving cutaway or cross-section with a fixed grid of labels that never change, and the only thing that animates is the named ingredient travelling below the surface while the named problem resolves. Where live footage is used, the labelled explainer graphic is pasted into the empty part of an otherwise unmoving frame.
rows.why_it_works: You watch the claim happen instead of hearing it. Because the labels never move, the eye has nothing to track except the mechanism, and a mechanism you can see reads as fact rather than marketing.

rows.name: Stunt funnel reveal
rows.what: The first act is an attention toll that has nothing to do with the offer — an absurd prop, an out-of-place stunt, a staged confrontation — carrying all the on-screen text and all the ugliness. Then a hard turn funnels it into the thing actually being sold, shot completely differently, carrying no text at all.
rows.why_it_works: The stunt buys attention no product shot could earn, and the production-quality gap at the seam is itself the reveal — the viewer feels they have been let in on something rather than sold to.

rows.name: Pinned-headline monologue
rows.what: One person, one seat, one room, one unbroken take to camera — and a single headline pinned in the top third that never changes for the entire runtime while rolling speech captions carry the argument underneath. No product, no cutaway, no demonstration, no second location.
rows.why_it_works: The pinned headline is a frame the viewer reads against every sentence spoken, so each line reassigns something under a claim they have already accepted. Nothing changes visually, so the only thing that can hold them is the argument — which is why the headline has to be the strongest line in the piece.

rows.name: Self-demo on the operator's own body
rows.what: The front camera is on the operator themselves, and their own face or body is both the demo surface and the payoff. One line opens the video — a craving line, a quoted comment, a claim — and either stays pinned or drops after the first beat; the rest is a wordless self-applied routine in one unchanging frame, ending on the surface visibly changed.
rows.why_it_works: Doing it to yourself on camera is the cheapest credible proof there is: nobody hired the face, and the before-state was volunteered. Because the frame never changes, the change in the skin is the only event, so it cannot be edited into existence.

rows.name: Era-stamped upgrade ladder
rows.what: Every beat carries a year stamp in the same fixed position, and the objects change with it — the obsolete method first, then 'Vs...', then the current or future year held for the rest of the runtime with the product doing the same job. The footage is stitched from visibly different sources with no continuity between rungs.
rows.why_it_works: The viewer agrees the old way was bad before the product is ever shown, so the product arrives as an upgrade they have already voted for rather than a pitch. The date stamp does that work in two words and needs no argument.

rows.name: Concern list with proof photos
rows.what: The same composite unit repeats at every beat — a fixed frame plus one big label naming a single concern plus a real photo of that exact concern composited into it. The caption changes every cut, the frame does not, and each named thing is paid off by a picture of the actual thing rather than by a claim.
rows.why_it_works: A list makes the viewer wait for their own item to come up, which buys the whole runtime. Each item lands as recognition, not persuasion, because the proof photo is the ordinary unretouched version they already own or already have.

rows.name: Wordless POV handoff transformation
rows.what: A POV arm reaches out of the bottom of frame and hands the product to a stranger, and the next beat is that stranger using it on camera. Zero on-screen text and no creator face at any point; the run repeats with new strangers in new places, or the crowd around the one stranger reacts to the result.
rows.why_it_works: A stranger who did not know the camera was coming cannot be coached, so their reaction in the second the product works is unfakeable. Keeping the creator entirely out of frame removes the only person the viewer would otherwise distrust.

rows.name: Pinned line, stranger sighting
rows.what: One unchanging line sits on screen while a handheld phone catches the product out in a real public place — the same subject sighted again and again in different parts of one venue, or worn into real transactions where unpaid strangers react to it. The repetition or the stranger's laugh is the payoff; nothing is demonstrated.
rows.why_it_works: A product spotted in the wild reads as evidence of a world rather than a pitch, and a laugh from someone who is not being paid is the one endorsement that cannot be bought. The pinned line just supplies the joke the sightings answer.

rows.name: Locked-macro debris lift
rows.what: One extreme-macro framing on a single site, absolutely locked, held for the whole runtime with no cuts and no second surface. rows.why_it_works: A room of people already treating the thing as an arrival is a stronger claim than any line, and it cannot be written. Because nothing is ever demonstrated or explained, there is nothing to disbelieve — the viewer is only shown who is there.

the wearers move through the room or the street, caught from across it
a tight jostled frame — bodies crossing between the lens and the subject
the scrum: onlookers with phones and cameras raised around them
a wider frame with the rope, the stanchions or the venue in shot

rows.name: Pinned line, reaction cut
rows.what: One setup line, usually ending on an open colon, is pinned word-for-word identical over borrowed spectacle footage for most of the runtime, and the last beat hard-cuts to one person's face in a completely different room under that same unchanged line. The footage is the illustration; the face is the answer the colon promised.
rows.why_it_works: An open colon is a sentence the viewer cannot close by reading, so the cut to a face lands as the completion of a thought rather than as a reaction shot. Because the line never changes, two unrelated sources read as one joke.
rows.evidence: [{"code": "DamBeiqJHdP", "author": "marquettdavon", "views": 499742, "line": "{audience} after seeing {the thing}: — pinned identical on all six beats, never completed"}]

beats: the pinned line lands over the borrowed footage, which plays in its own unchanging frame
the borrowed act escalates on its own terms, line unchanged
it keeps escalating — nothing is added and nothing is cut to
the spectacle peaks
hard cut: one person's face in an interior room, flat and unreacting, the same line still pinned
extra.text_behaviour: one line pinned word-for-word in the identical position on every single beat including the final cut, ending on an open colon and never completed in words
extra.camera: whatever camera the borrowed footage came with, held full-frame and uncut for most of the runtime, then a hard cut to a fixed front-camera close in an ordinary room that does not move

rows.name: Locked frame, screen readout
rows.what: One absolutely locked frame with a person in it who never turns to camera or leaves their seat, a caption pinned unchanged for the entire runtime, and a screen inside the frame that is the only thing that changes — a document, a dashboard, a monitor rig — walked through section by section while the viewer reads it over their shoulder.
rows.why_it_works: It is the inverse of a demo: because the frame and the caption are both constants, the screen is the only moving part, so the deck becomes the argument. Reading something over someone's shoulder feels like access rather than a pitch.
rows.evidence: [{"code": "Db4M9M8iI_B", "author": "cortez_seay", "views": 1894115, "line": "It IS this serious 💔🥺"}]

beats: the locked frame opens with the caption pinned and the screen on a title or a single word
the first section arrives on screen — a heading, a block of text, a small grid of evidence
section two, the person gesturing at the screen without ever turning to camera
section three, the stack now visibly longer than the runtime
back to a bare title screen or a final readout, the frame and the caption unchanged
extra.text_behaviour: one short line pinned in the identical position from first frame to last, never changed and never argued; everything else that gets read belongs to the document inside the frame
extra.camera: absolutely locked for the whole runtime — same framing, same background, same light — with the subject filling one side of frame and the screen the other; no cut, no reframe, no cutaway

rows.name: Multicam monologue with crowd cutaway
rows.what: One continuous live take of a performer talking to a real room, covered from four or more camera positions — tight close, full-stage wide, audience reverse, from behind the crowd — with word-synced speech captions running under every angle and a cutaway to the audience reacting placed exactly where the line lands.
rows.why_it_works: The reaction cutaway is proof the line worked on people who were actually there, which no caption can claim. Multi-angle coverage of one take is what makes the room read as real rather than staged, and the captions keep the speech legible with the sound off so the reaction means something.

the same close angle holds while the setup lands
cut to the full-stage wide — the venue and the room become visible
reverse onto the audience at the punchline: real people visibly reacting
back to a tighter or darker angle for the next run
from behind the crowd, the performer small and the room around them
extra.text_behaviour: burned-in word-synced speech captions, centre-low, running continuously under every angle with the currently spoken words highlighted; nothing pinned and nothing authored
extra.camera: one continuous live take covered from four or more fixed positions — tight close, full-stage wide, audience reverse, from the back of the room — each near-locked; the edit changes angle rather than the camera moving

rows.name: Operator service montage
rows.what: A professional performs a multi-step service ON A CLIENT, shot third-person, with each product labelled on screen as it is used. The operator is an authority with hands on someone else's face; the viewer watches as the person in the chair, not as the person filming. Opens on the trade's own known ritual (the clippers, the wash) before any product appears, which buys the procedure its credibility.
rows.why_it_works: Every claim arrives as a caption on a procedure already underway, so nothing is being argued — it is being labelled. And because the subject is a paying client rather than the creator, the viewer has somebody to identify with who did not choose the product: the endorsement is the professional's, the experience is the stranger's, and the viewer is neither, which is a comfortable place to watch from.

rows.name: Stranger answer montage
rows.what: The creator states the question to camera, then approaches strangers in public and lets their unscripted answers carry the whole argument. Every word is burned in as rolling captions because the audio is street audio. The creator never makes the claim — the strangers make it for him, and the more reluctant or unpolished they sound, the better it works.
rows.why_it_works: The persuasion belongs to people with nothing to gain. A creator saying women notice your skin is an ad; four strangers saying it unprompted is evidence. The awkwardness is load-bearing — a stranger hesitating, or giving a blunt answer the creator did not want, is the proof that nothing was scripted.

first approach, caught mid-walk, question asked cold
two to four more answers cut tight, the captions carrying them
optional: a meme or reaction insert on the funniest answer
the answer that lands the point, given the most room
optional: the handoff — product given to the stranger, explained on the spot
extra.text_behaviour: burned-in rolling captions on every line of speech, question and answer both, in the creator's own rough typing; no headline, no pinned claim — the captions are transcription, not copy
extra.camera: handheld, vertical, medium on the stranger with the creator's shoulder or mic in frame; wide when walking up so the approach reads as real; daylight public space, no lighting, ambient sound

rows.name: Storytelling
rows.what: One named person with one reason, told as a story: who he was before, the turn (he found out it was never his fault), who he is after — the beats are the story's, not a pitch's, and the product enters where the turn happens. Aimed at a buyer who already wants the outcome.
rows.why_it_works: One swiped brand runs 100,000+ customers off 44 ads because every ad is one person's reason for switching, told in her own words; story and intent do the work volume does for everyone else.
rows.examples: A swiped brand's story ads — one person, one reason each; a brand's story block in brand-identity/story.md (SPINE · BEFORE · TURN · AFTER, the tellers)

rows.name: Timeline turn
rows.what: Four beats. 1 PAST — open on a moment the viewer lived (a real customer line about then, from the avatar's language bank), shot so it looks like then. 2 RELATE — the problem they have now started back there; they see their own history. 3 THE TURN — one moment where the timeline changes: the younger self gets told, the tape rewinds, the 'continue?' screen. 4 FORWARD — the product is the new timeline; the last ask is the click.
rows.why_it_works: Most people don't think about the future, they live in the past. Starting where they already are lets them relate before any claim; the turn hands them the moment to change it, and that is what moves them forward.
rows.evidence: the owner 2026-10-03: 'build nostalgic formats and classic formats that people actually remember… program for the past to bring them in a place they can relate to, and from there you give them a moment to change the timeline' · 'nothing more nothing less — real life experiences they go through and experience, and also what they watch'. · the owner 2026-10-03: 'whatever the actual research shows then we roll with it… nothing to do with my taste.'
rows.note: RESEARCH (2026-10-03): real past memories (hand-sorted) are rare in two brands' language banks — about 1 line in 600 to 2,000 — present but rare; one brand's own 'growing up' post had millions of views. The one swiped structure on this idea with proof is era-stamped-upgrade-ladder (29.96M views). named by the owner 2026-10-03; definition is the machine's, review pending. Rule: the past anchor is a real customer line from the avatar's language bank, the era references come from the avatar profile's cultural-relevance section and age band — nothing invented. Grief lines (a parent who passed) are never used as an anchor.
